benchmark_name: Seed-conditioned graph explanation retrieval pilot v2 (release annotations)
annotation_status: Provisional AI-assisted draft relevance labels; not independently reviewed or held out

protocol.query_inputs: Question text and identical known seed IDs/names; no answer labels
protocol.graph_ranking: Existing shortest paths; unique edges ranked by hop then ID
protocol.tfidf_ranking: TF-IDF cosine similarity, then chunk ID; zero-score hits omitted
protocol.aggregation: Macro average over distinct questions, not participants
protocol.latency: Single warm-process query time; TF-IDF fitting excluded; descriptive only
protocol.interval: Paired query bootstrap, 2000 replicates, seed 20261107; not external validity

limitations: This is a pilot on graph-derived text chunks, not original paper passages or clinical truth.
Questions and relevance labels were authored during development; independent blinded review is still required.
Labels express intended relevance within the current graph, not scientific validity of its relationships. Unlisted chunks are provisionally judged nonrelevant.
The shared corpus comes from the graph, so this comparison is conditional on that representation and may favour graph retrieval.
Both methods receive known seed-node metadata; results do not measure entity linking or open-ended document search.
The baseline is lexical TF-IDF, not dense-vector or hybrid RAG. Report generation and clinical usefulness are not evaluated.
Small, related questions limit uncertainty estimates. The bootstrap intervals are descriptive, not independent validation.

questions.rationale: The question requests the pause-to-review branch, not the questionnaire or concentration branch. Relevance is to the stored explanation, not causality.

questions.question: How does the stored pause-ratio interpretation connect to difficulty concentrating and questionnaire content?
questions.rationale: The concentration branch and PHQ-8 item membership answer this question; risk and follow-up edges alone do not.

questions.rationale: These connect the measured descriptor to the fatigue interpretation and questionnaire node. They do not establish subjective fatigue from RMS.

questions.rationale: The two interpretive links address the question; they are not validation of the frame-level jitter proxy.

questions.rationale: These two relations provide the requested conceptual chain, without claiming clinical confirmation.

questions.question: What contextual interpretation connects high MFCC 2 variability with spectral shift and depressed mood?
questions.rationale: The spectral descriptor and requires_context_for relation answer the local interpretation question.

questions.question: Which links connect low MFCC 3 mean through spectral shift and depressed mood to the questionnaire?
questions.rationale: All three relations are needed for the requested stored path to questionnaire content.

questions.question: Which interpretation links high MFCC 4 variability to depressed mood, and how is that relationship qualified?

benchmark_snapshot.revision_note: Release graph descriptions corrected. Edge IDs, questions and provisional relevance sets retained; no independent relevance review performed. Historical v1 is archived separately.

corpus_snapshot.text: biomarker:high_jitter High Jitter Elevated pitch-period instability across retained voiced frames. This implemented proxy is not conventional cycle-to-cycle jitter and does not establish arousal or a clinical symptom. indicates concept:vocal_instability Vocal Instability Irregular or unstable vocal production.  Speech-analysis reviews associate perturbation and voice-source instability with depression-relevant vocal control changes. Cummins et al. (2015) Low et al. (2020)

biomarker:high_mfcc_1_mean High MFCC 1 Mean A shifted first cepstral coefficient may reflect broad spectral-energy changes in the voice. indicates concept:spectral_shift Spectral Shift Changes in cepstral or spectral balance that can cue altered voice quality.  MFCCs are widely used spectral descriptors in psychiatric speech assessment, but they require semantic mapping for interpretation. Al Hanai et al. (2018) Low et al. (2020)

biomarker:high_mfcc_2_std High MFCC 2 Variability Greater spectral-shape variability can indicate inconsistent articulation or affective instability. indicates concept:spectral_shift Spectral Shift Changes in cepstral or spectral balance that can cue altered voice quality.  MFCC variability captures spectral-shape changes that may reflect altered speech production or affective expression. Al Hanai et al. (2018) Low et al. (2020)

biomarker:high_mfcc_4_std High MFCC 4 Variability Higher mid-cepstral variability may reflect unstable speech production across the recording. indicates concept:spectral_shift Spectral Shift Changes in cepstral or spectral balance that can cue altered voice quality.  Mid-cepstral variability is retained as a calibrated spectral marker and interpreted only through graph context. Al Hanai et al. (2018) Low et al. (2020)

biomarker:high_pause_ratio High Pause Ratio Frequent or extended pauses may reflect hesitation, cognitive load, avoidance, or disrupted speech flow. indicates concept:speech_disruption Speech Disruption Interrupted, hesitant, or slowed speech flow.  Longer silence and pause behaviour are commonly reported in speech-based depression screening work. Al Hanai et al. (2018) Cummins et al. (2015) Low et al. (2020)

biomarker:high_pitch_mean High Mean Pitch Raised average pitch can be consistent with affective tension or altered activation, depending on speaker baseline. may_support symptom:psychomotor_change Psychomotor Slowing or Agitation   Mean pitch is treated as an activation-sensitive prosodic marker requiring contextual interpretation. Cummins et al. (2015) Low et al. (2020)

biomarker:high_pitch_variability High Pitch Variability Large pitch variation may suggest unstable vocal control during depression-relevant affective states. indicates concept:vocal_instability Vocal Instability Irregular or unstable vocal production.  Pitch and frequency variability are repeatedly discussed as depression-relevant prosodic markers, although direction depends on context and speaker baseline. Cummins et al. (2015) Low et al. (2020) Mundt et al. (2007)

biomarker:low_energy Low Vocal Energy Reduced vocal intensity may indicate flattened expression, fatigue, withdrawal, or low activation. indicates concept:reduced_expressivity Reduced Expressivity Lower vocal activation or flattened prosodic expression.  Reduced vocal intensity and energy are commonly treated as markers of flattened affect, fatigue, or reduced activation. Al Hanai et al. (2018) Cummins et al. (2015) Low et al. (2020) Mundt et al. (2007)

biomarker:low_mfcc_3_mean Low MFCC 3 Mean A low third cepstral coefficient may indicate altered spectral balance requiring contextual review. indicates concept:spectral_shift Spectral Shift Changes in cepstral or spectral balance that can cue altered voice quality.  MFCC coefficients are model-facing spectral biomarkers; the graph maps them cautiously to qualitative spectral shift rather than direct diagnosis. Al Hanai et al. (2018) Low et al. (2020)

biomarker:low_pitch_mean Low Mean Pitch Lowered average pitch can appear with reduced expressivity, fatigue, or psychomotor slowing. may_support concept:reduced_expressivity Reduced Expressivity Lower vocal activation or flattened prosodic expression.  Lower pitch or reduced prosodic activation can appear with reduced expressivity and fatigue, but requires speaker-context review. Cummins et al. (2015) Low et al. (2020) Mundt et al. (2007)

biomarker:low_speech_rate Low Speech Rate Reduced words per second may reflect slowed speech production, psychomotor slowing, or reduced verbal fluency. may_support concept:reduced_expressivity Reduced Expressivity Lower vocal activation or flattened prosodic expression.  Slower speech rate is linked to reduced verbal fluency, psychomotor slowing, and depression severity in prior speech studies. Al Hanai et al. (2018) Cummins et al. (2015) Low et al. (2020) Mundt et al. (2007)

biomarker:low_speech_rate Low Speech Rate Reduced words per second may reflect slowed speech production, psychomotor slowing, or reduced verbal fluency. indicates concept:speech_disruption Speech Disruption Interrupted, hesitant, or slowed speech flow.  Slower speech rate is linked to reduced verbal fluency, psychomotor slowing, and depression severity in prior speech studies. Al Hanai et al. (2018) Cummins et al. (2015) Low et al. (2020) Mundt et al. (2007)

concept:reduced_expressivity Reduced Expressivity  may_support symptom:fatigue Fatigue or Low Energy   Reduced expressivity connects low energy and prosodic flattening to fatigue or low activation in clinical interpretation. Al Hanai et al. (2018) Cummins et al. (2015) Low et al. (2020) Mundt et al. (2007)

concept:spectral_shift Spectral Shift  requires_context_for symptom:depressed_mood Depressed Mood   Spectral features are useful biomarkers but need clinical context before linking them to mood symptoms. Low et al. (2020) Cummins et al. (2015)

concept:speech_disruption Speech Disruption  contributes_to risk:depression_screening_risk Depression Screening Risk Non-diagnostic signal that depression-relevant speech patterns may be present.  Speech disruption, pausing, and slowed rhythm are linked to depression-relevant interview behaviour. Al Hanai et al. (2018) Cummins et al. (2015) Low et al. (2020)

concept:speech_disruption Speech Disruption  may_support symptom:concentration_difficulty Difficulty Concentrating   Speech disruption, pausing, and slowed rhythm are linked to depression-relevant interview behaviour. Al Hanai et al. (2018) Cummins et al. (2015) Low et al. (2020)

concept:vocal_instability Vocal Instability  contributes_to risk:depression_screening_risk Depression Screening Risk Non-diagnostic signal that depression-relevant speech patterns may be present.  Voice instability can contribute to depression-relevant screening evidence but is not diagnostic alone. Cummins et al. (2015) Low et al. (2020)

concept:vocal_instability Vocal Instability  may_support symptom:psychomotor_change Psychomotor Slowing or Agitation   Voice instability can contribute to depression-relevant screening evidence but is not diagnostic alone. Cummins et al. (2015) Low et al. (2020)
